options.text: It guarantees indexing by inserting keywords into every heading.
It replaces useful content with technical settings that determine rankings.
It helps search engines understand content and helps people discover the website and decide whether to visit. I apply it to useful content, with technical access and a clear search presentation.
It pays Google to place selected pages above competitors.
Google recommends evaluating all changes immediately after publishing.
Every SEO change takes exactly six months to affect results.

Google says effects can take hours to months, and generally advises waiting a few weeks to assess benefit. I establish a baseline and allow time for recrawling and processing; I do not promise an exact improvement date.
Every successful change must improve rankings within 24 hours.
Every site must submit a sitemap before Google can index it.

No. Google can discover pages through links, and the Starter Guide calls a sitemap optional. It is useful for communicating important URLs, particularly when discovery through links is weaker, but does not guarantee indexing.
Sitemaps replace the need for any discoverable internal links.
A sitemap guarantees that its listed URLs will rank.
Use URL Inspection to examine the rendered page and accessibility of its resources. Check CSS and JavaScript blocking and location-dependent responses, rather than trusting only my browser view.
Assume valid HTML proves Google accessed every required resource.
Compare only the page displayed in your own logged-in browser.
Check keyword density instead of Google's rendered page.
Folder names guarantee a ranking boost for every contained page.
Every directory forces Google to crawl its URLs daily.
Directory structure prevents Google from choosing canonical URLs.
For users, it clarifies structure. At larger scale, it can help Google learn that different groups change at different frequencies. It is not a reason to rebuild every healthy site immediately.

Routine duplication on one's own site is not itself a spam violation or cause of a manual action. I consolidate where appropriate because duplicates can confuse users and waste crawling, and distinguish this from copied or manipulative content.
Duplicate URLs improve quality because Google rewards more copies.
Google always excludes the entire site after detecting two duplicate pages.
Every duplicate product URL automatically triggers a manual action.
Redirects and canonical declarations are always identical for users and Google.
Canonical tags redirect users to the preferred URL automatically.
Use a redirect only when both URLs must remain independently accessible.

Use a redirect when the redundant URL should send users to the preferred page. If the alternate URL needs to remain accessible, a canonical declaration can indicate the preferred representative. Google ultimately performs canonical selection.
No. Understand audience language and use relevant terminology naturally. Google's language matching can relate a page to queries without every exact phrase appearing.
Repeat all keyword permutations to satisfy a fixed density requirement.
Google understands only exact strings and cannot match related terminology.
Every exact keyword variation must appear before Google can match it.

No. Title links have several inputs, including title elements and headings; snippets usually come from page text and can sometimes use a meta description. I improve accurate inputs and inspect actual presentation.
Google must display the title and description exactly as supplied.
Google creates every snippet exclusively from the meta description.
Visible headings can never influence a search result's title link.

Sharp relevant images placed near explanatory text, with descriptive alt text explaining their relationship to the page. The guide focuses on discoverability and understanding, not a prescribed keyword density.
Place images away from related text to avoid semantic confusion.
Replace descriptive image text with a fixed keyword-density formula.
Repeat the target keyword in alt text regardless of the image.
A page with an incidental video is always equivalent to a watch page.
Hide the video behind interaction and omit descriptive text.
Use unrelated video titles because Google ignores their descriptions.

Create a high-quality video, give it a standalone page where the video is the main focus, add relevant supporting text, and write descriptive video titles and descriptions. Then consult Google's video-specific guidance.
User-generated links must always be treated as the publisher's endorsements.
All external links must be nofollow, including trusted editorial references.

The guide recommends linking to trusted relevant resources normally and qualifying links you cannot endorse or that come from users. Additional official guidance prefers sponsored for paid placements and ugc for user contributions.
Paid placements should use ordinary links without any qualification.
A keyword-rich .com domain guarantees higher rankings worldwide.
Google gives every generic TLD the same fixed geographic target.

No. Domain and path keywords alone have little ranking effect; select names for the business. Country-code domains can help communicate a geographic target, but generic TLDs have no universal advantage.
Any country-code domain is always a stronger global ranking choice.
A minimum word count determines quality regardless of usefulness.
Google requires one identical heading count for every content type.
Every ranking page needs exactly 1,500 words and three H2 headings.
There is no ideal ranking word count or magic number of headings. Use enough detail and a logical accessible structure to satisfy the audience. Do not pad articles to meet an invented threshold.
Google no longer uses any link-based ranking system.
It remains one fundamental algorithm involving links, but Google uses many signals. Treating rankings as a PageRank-only problem misses relevance, quality, and the wider search process.
PageRank is the only system Google uses to rank results.
PageRank guarantees relevance without considering the query or content.
An advertising account guarantees organic indexing of its landing pages.
No. Legitimate promotion can improve awareness and discovery. Google does not accept money for organic inclusion, higher rankings, or faster crawling.
Buying Google Ads directly increases organic rankings.
Promotion fees can purchase more frequent organic crawling from Google.
Stop monitoring once the initial audit has been completed.

Monitor Search Console, keep content and technical configurations maintained, plan changes such as migrations carefully, and add appropriate structured data for eligible search features while staying current with official guidance.
Replace ongoing maintenance with a guaranteed permanent ranking promise.
Add all available markup types regardless of the page's content.
Google serves pages directly from sitemaps without evaluating relevance.
Google indexes every submitted URL without crawling or analyzing it.

Google discovers URLs through known pages, links, and sitemaps. Googlebot may crawl and render them, including JavaScript. Google then analyzes content, groups similar pages and selects canonicals, and may store information in its index. For a query, it serves relevant, high-quality results based on many signals and user context. None of the stages is guaranteed.
Google ranks first, then discovers URLs, and skips indexing.
Discovery and crawling both mean the page has been downloaded.
A discovered URL is automatically indexed without being requested.
Crawling means ranking a URL for every relevant query.

Discovery means Google knows a URL exists. Crawling means it actually requests and downloads the content. A discovered URL can remain uncrawled because of scheduling, access restrictions, or server issues.
New pages must appear in a sitemap because links cannot reveal them.
A known category or hub page can link to it, another website can link to it, or its URL can appear in a submitted sitemap. Google also knows URLs it has visited before.
Only a paid submission to Google can reveal a new page.
A page cannot be discovered until someone searches its exact URL.
Google never executes JavaScript when processing pages.
Google runs every browser API with the user's existing cookies and permissions.
JavaScript execution guarantees that every dynamic page will be indexed.

Yes, it renders using a recent Chrome version. That does not mean every JavaScript implementation works reliably for Search; resources, rendering limitations, and how content appears still need checking.
Only low keyword density can stop a discovered URL being crawled.
Every discovered URL is guaranteed an immediate crawl.
A crawl restriction prevents discovery and removes all ranking signals automatically.
It may be blocked by robots.txt, unavailable without login, affected by server or network problems, or simply not selected for crawling yet. Discovery alone is insufficient.
They indicate server trouble and can cause Google to slow crawling to avoid overload. I would investigate server health before interpreting reduced crawl activity as a content problem.
Server errors are ignored because Google crawls only cached copies.
A 500 response acts as a permanent redirect to the homepage.
Repeated 500 responses tell Google to crawl more aggressively.
Indexing consists only of downloading the original HTML response.
Indexing guarantees the page will rank for its target keywords.

Google interprets text and important attributes, images and videos, identifies similar-page clusters, selects a canonical representative, and gathers language, locality, and usability information that may be stored in the index.
Google indexes a page by counting keywords without analyzing other content.
A canonical is the page with the highest paid advertising spend.
The canonical is always the first URL the publisher created.

It is the representative Google selects from a group of pages with similar content, generally the one that may be shown in results. Other pages in the cluster can be alternate versions served in some contexts.
Canonical selection permanently prevents any alternate from appearing.
A crawled page is unindexed only when its owner has not paid Google.
Possible causes in this article include low quality, robots meta restrictions, and design that makes indexing difficult. Google also explicitly does not promise to index every page it processes.
Sitemap inclusion overrides noindex and guarantees indexing.
Every successfully crawled page must enter Google's index.
Low visibility proves Google has never crawled the indexed URL.
An indexed page must appear identically for every user and query.
Indexing guarantees a first-page position for the target keyword.

Indexing establishes potential availability, not query relevance or a ranking position. Low relevance, quality, serving restrictions, and the query's context can keep it from appearing where we expect.
Differences are caused only by whether the website bought advertising.
Device and location never affect relevance in Google Search.
Every searcher receives identical results regardless of location or language.
Google can consider location, language, and device. For a local-intent query, businesses near one searcher can be more relevant than those near another.
The features depend on the user's query and the information likely to satisfy it. The article contrasts bicycle repair shops with modern bicycle images.
Every query always displays exactly the same search features.
Image and local results are selected only by the publisher's preference.
A sitemap setting determines which feature appears for every query.
A premium submission fee guarantees higher organic rankings.
An advertiser can pay Google for faster organic crawling.
No. Google explicitly rejects both claims. Advertising and organic search processes should be explained separately.
Paying an approved agency buys privileged access to organic ranking systems.

Submission can help discovery. I would show whether the URL was crawled, indexed, selected as canonical, and relevant to the target query, then address the actual bottleneck. Submission is not a ranking guarantee.
Add backlinks immediately because submission rules out all technical issues.
Submission guarantees ranking, so no diagnostic investigation is needed.
Resubmit repeatedly until Google guarantees first-page visibility.
Assess quality solely by reaching a fixed word count.
Ignore accuracy if the content has a high automated SEO score.

I would assess original value, completeness for the task, accuracy, source credibility, readability, audience relevance, and whether visitors can achieve their goal. I would use the page's self-assessment questions and independent feedback, rather than word count as a quality proxy.
Treat keyword repetition and publication volume as proof of usefulness.
Experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness. Google says trust is the most important aspect, with the others contributing to it.
Experience, originality, keyword density and trustworthiness.
Expertise, engagement, authority and technical speed.
Engagement, efficiency, automation and traffic.
Google publishes an E-E-A-T score that directly fixes positions.
E-E-A-T is one numeric ranking factor controlled by adding a byline.
E-E-A-T is irrelevant because no quality-related signals are used.

Not as a single specific factor. Google's automated systems use a mixture of signals that can identify these qualities. I would explain the quality concepts without claiming that adding a byline produces a direct numerical ranking boost.
Every page requires a certified academic expert as its author.

No. Some pages are valuable because of first-hand experience, and not every useful task requires specialist expertise. Higher-stakes YMYL information requires greater accuracy and appropriate expertise; authorship must always be truthful.
First-hand experience can never support useful content.
Fabricated expert credentials are acceptable when the writing is polished.

Subjects that can significantly affect health, financial stability, safety, or societal welfare. Google gives greater weight to content aligned with strong E-E-A-T in these areas, and stresses highly accurate information consistent with expert consensus.
YMYL concerns only websites that directly accept payments.
YMYL content is evaluated with less emphasis on accuracy and trust.
Any topic with a long article is automatically YMYL.
Each individual rating is immediately inserted into live ranking calculations.
Raters apply manual penalties to every page they consider weak.
A quality rater can directly change a page's ranking position.
No. Raters evaluate whether Google's systems produce good results; they do not control individual rankings, and their feedback is not directly inserted into ranking algorithms.

Content serves an intended audience, reflects useful knowledge or experience, fits the site's purpose, helps people complete a task, and leaves them satisfied even if they came directly rather than through Search.
Select topics only by volume and ignore whether visitors complete their task.
Publish primarily to capture traffic even without a relevant audience.
Optimize for crawler patterns even if the content disappoints readers.
A satisfying answer is suspicious unless it reaches a fixed length.
Clear sourcing is a warning sign because it distracts ranking systems.

Publishing unrelated topics for traffic, summarizing without added value, excessive automation, chasing trends unrelated to the audience, artificial date changes, and targeting an invented word count. These should trigger reassessment of the production strategy.
Original research and audience relevance are search-engine-first warning signs.
Bulk deletion automatically improves rankings by making the site look fresh.

Google says bulk removal or addition mainly to create a freshness impression does not provide that general benefit. I would update, merge, or remove pages according to relevance, accuracy, usefulness, and business purpose.
Updating dates without changing content produces a general freshness boost.
Every old page must be removed regardless of usefulness or relevance.
Judge the cause solely from a third-party domain score.
Assume a penalty and buy backlinks without checking affected queries.

First identify which pages and types of searches lost visibility. Then evaluate those pages against the quality and audience questions and get independent feedback. I would not assume the cause before examining the evidence.
Rewrite every page before identifying where the decline occurred.
Product information behind tabs is excluded from the page's purpose.

Anything that directly fulfills the page's purpose: text or media, calculators and tools, forum discussion or reviews, relevant tabbed content, and visible headings. A calculator's functional value can be its main content.
Interactive tools and relevant user contributions can never be main content.
Only the article's opening paragraph qualifies as main content.
Word count, keyword density, backlink count and page age.
AI detection score, schema count, domain age and image count.
Effort, originality, talent or skill, and accuracy. These concern how effectively the page fulfills its purpose, not a mandatory format or minimum word count.
Speed, ad revenue, title length and posting frequency.
No. Attribution does not substitute for original effort or added value. I would contribute evidence, analysis, testing, or a useful application rather than republishing a lightly rewritten summary.
Changing synonyms proves originality without new information or work.
Attribution alone makes any automated summary original and high effort.
A rewritten summary needs no added value if every paragraph cites a source.
Information behind any tab can never count as main content.
Tabbed specifications must be moved to images to count as main content.
Yes. The guide explicitly includes tabbed or expanded sections that fulfill the page's purpose. I would still verify that the actual implementation exposes the intended information to Google.
Only text visible before any interaction can fulfill a product page's purpose.

Identify the real reviewer and relevant background; document the testing method, products, results, and evidence; and ensure the review exists to help a buyer make a decision. Avoid fabricated authors and unsupported claims.
Use synthetic credentials and generic claims instead of evidence of testing.
Explain only the target keywords and planned ranking position.
Invent an expert author and omit the testing method.
Every use of AI requires one universal Google label on every page.

The guide recommends context and disclosures where readers would reasonably expect an explanation of substantial automation. It does not prescribe one universal label. Merchant Center has separate specific requirements for certain AI-generated product data.
AI production should never be explained, even when readers expect context.
Editorial disclosure replaces Merchant Center's specific metadata requirements.
False credentials are acceptable when AI-generated content is accurate.

Using them to fabricate human expert identities is deceptive. Google explicitly treats fabricated creator profiles and credentials as untrustworthy. Real provenance and honest expertise are the appropriate direction.
Invented expert identities improve trust if their portraits look realistic.
Google requires synthetic author photos to demonstrate expertise.
Traditional SEO has no relevance to Google's generative search experiences.

No. Google says these experiences rely on its core Search ranking and quality systems. I would prioritize technical eligibility, distinctive useful content, a good experience, relevant business data, and measurement.
Only a proprietary AI schema can make a website visible now.
AI features bypass Search's ranking and quality systems entirely.

Retrieval-augmented generation grounds a response in relevant pages retrieved from the Search index, using Google's core systems. It can improve freshness and accuracy and provide supporting links, rather than relying entirely on a model's training memory.
RAG is a paid system that purchases Google ranking positions.
RAG creates responses solely from model memory without retrieving pages.
RAG requires a separate page for every possible related query.
Fan-out means excluding all related queries from information retrieval.
Fan-out means publishing one page for every keyword permutation.
Fan-out is a schema field that guarantees an AI citation.

The model issues multiple related queries to gather supporting information for the user's original request. It expands information retrieval; it is not a recommendation to publish a separate page for every variant.
Generic summaries of common advice automatically qualify as distinctive value.
Non-commodity content is defined only by exceeding a minimum word count.

Information with distinctive value, such as original testing, first-hand experience, expert interpretation, or a unique perspective. A generic rewording of common advice provides less unique value than a documented real-world case.
Replacing words with synonyms creates original first-hand expertise.
Only llms.txt is required; indexing and snippets do not matter.

The current guide says it must be indexed, eligible for Search with a snippet, meet technical requirements, and be included in Search generative AI features through Search Console. Eligibility does not guarantee appearance.
Adding AI schema guarantees appearance even when the page is noindex.
Every indexed page appears in AI features regardless of the inclusion control.
llms.txt guarantees a ranking boost in Google Search.
llms.txt is mandatory for appearing in Google's AI features.

No. This guide explicitly says Google Search ignores it, including for its AI capabilities. It can be useful to a different system that uses it, but it is not a Google visibility requirement or ranking boost.
Google uses llms.txt to replace its ordinary crawling and indexing process.
Google cannot understand more than one topic on a page.
No. Google can understand several topics within one page and select relevant material. I would choose sections and length for readers rather than comply with an invented AI chunk size.
Short chunks guarantee AI citations regardless of usefulness or indexing.
Every article must be split into exactly 100-word AI chunks.
Only pages with all schema.org types are eligible for AI features.
Standard structured data guarantees inclusion in AI Overviews.
No. The guide says structured data is not required for generative AI search and there is no special AI schema.org markup. Appropriate standard markup remains useful for rich-result eligibility.
A proprietary AIOverview schema is mandatory for every supporting page.
Not primarily to manipulate AI responses or rankings. The guide warns this can violate scaled content abuse policy. I would identify genuine audience needs and avoid redundant low-value pages.
High page volume by itself guarantees better AI visibility.
Publish every possible query variant even when no page adds value.
Scaled content abuse rules do not apply to AI optimization.
Accessibility is irrelevant because Google requires only AI-specific Markdown.
Perfect markup guarantees visibility regardless of content or crawl access.
Any semantic HTML error automatically excludes a page from AI features.

No. The guide recommends semantic HTML where useful for readability and accessibility, but does not require perfect markup. Crawl access, rendering, actual content, and experience still need attention.
Replace product and business information with repeated AI keywords.
Treat optional merchant experiences as mandatory ranking factors.
Omit feeds and business details because AI responses cannot use them.

Maintain useful distinctive site content, technical access, relevant Merchant Center data and Google Business Profile information. Consider optional merchant experiences when they fit the business rather than treating them as required ranking factors.
Infer official AI visibility from a vendor's alleged internal Google score.
Assume the linked AI report measures every click, CTR and query metric.

The current guide points to the Generative AI performance report. The linked Search help page documents AI Overviews and AI Mode impressions, with page, country, date, and device breakdowns. I would combine that visibility evidence with separate business outcome measurement.
Count llms.txt requests as proof of impressions in AI Overviews.
Use the AI exclusion setting to remove all ordinary Search listings.
Assume every child property ignores all parent inclusion settings.

The linked current Search Console documentation provides a Search generative AI inclusion control. It covers specified AI features and does not act as a ranking or inclusion signal for other parts of Search. Check inheritance and the actual property setting.
Apply noindex everywhere because no separate inclusion control exists.
AEO and GEO always require special Google AI files and schema.
Guaranteed AI citations become valid when marketed as GEO.
A new acronym makes official Search guidance unnecessary.

They describe optimization for answer or generative engines, but Google treats optimization for its AI experiences as SEO. I would evaluate the specific claim and platform, rather than accept that a new label requires unsupported tactics.
Supporting an emerging agent protocol guarantees higher Google rankings.
AI agents can only read model memory and never interact with websites.
An agentic experience is a fixed organic ranking score for AI citations.

An AI agent performs tasks for a user, such as booking or comparing products. It may inspect screenshots, DOM content, or accessibility structure. Relevant sites can explore agent-friendly practices and emerging protocols without presenting them as guaranteed ranking improvements.
Any AI-generated page is guaranteed to rank once it is published.
AI content is exempt from all quality and spam policies.
Google prohibits every page that used generative AI in production.

No. It can assist useful research and structuring original content. The problem is low-value or manipulative production, especially many pages without user value, and failure to meet Search Essentials and spam policies.
Publishing more pages guarantees quality even when they repeat existing content.
Only manually written low-value pages can violate scaled content abuse policy.
AI-generated pages are automatically compliant regardless of user value.

Using AI or similar tools to produce many pages without adding value for users may violate the policy. I would evaluate purpose and actual value rather than assume that changing the production tool removes the risk.
AI output is inherently factual and requires no human checking.
Review is unnecessary when the content passes an AI detection tool.
Only spelling needs checking because models retrieve all facts accurately.
Models can generate plausible but inaccurate claims. The current guide says to manually fact-check and review all generated material for accuracy and trustworthiness before publication.
Only body copy needs review; metadata cannot affect search presentation.
Structured data and alt text are exempt from accuracy requirements.
Title elements, meta descriptions, structured data, and image alt text. These fields can be inaccurate or misleading and can appear in search experiences.
Generated titles should be trusted even when they contradict the page.
Add unsupported facts to markup to qualify for more features.
Skip feature-specific policies if an AI generated the structured data.

Check it against the real page, general structured-data guidelines, and feature-specific policies, then validate the markup. Do not assume generated JSON is accurate because it is syntactically valid.
Accept generated markup whenever the JSON parses successfully.

Context that helps them understand how and why automation was used, where reasonably expected. The general guide recommends explaining the process; Merchant Center has separate explicit labeling and metadata requirements.
Claim a human expert wrote the content whenever AI generated it.
Never disclose substantial automation, even when readers reasonably expect context.
One generic AI notice replaces every product-data provenance requirement.
Add a canonical tag to the image instead of its IPTC source type.
An alt attribute alone replaces the required provenance metadata.
Strip all source metadata to make generated images look human-created.
The required IPTC DigitalSourceType metadata must identify the AI origin, including TrainedAlgorithmicMedia. Preserve embedded source metadata rather than stripping it during optimization.
Put the AI provenance solely in robots.txt rather than the product attributes.
Add noindex to generated titles instead of the required structured fields.
Use ordinary product fields without identifying generated text separately.

The article says to identify them separately. The linked Merchant Center policy specifies structured_title and structured_description, using digital_source_type=trained_algorithmic_media and the generated content.
No. They help raters evaluate the quality of Search systems. The AI-content page specifically cautions that ratings do not directly influence ranking and the guidelines are not a first-place recipe.
Every page rated highly must appear first for all related queries.
The guidelines are a guaranteed recipe for first-place ranking.
Rater scores directly assign ranking positions to individual pages.

robots.txt controls crawling. noindex controls indexing when Google can fetch and process it. Blocking the URL first can prevent Google from seeing its noindex instruction; private information should use access restrictions.
Combining Disallow and noindex guarantees immediate removal.
robots.txt provides the same privacy protection as authentication.
robots.txt controls indexing while noindex controls only crawling.
Important rendering resources never need to be crawlable.
Blocking essential resources guarantees that crawling shifts to useful URLs.

Not if Google needs it to render and understand important pages. The guide explicitly requires access to important resources. Target redundant or unnecessary crawl requests after diagnosing the actual problem.
Block all CSS even when Google needs it to understand the page.
Every sitemap timestamp should change daily regardless of actual updates.
priority assigns the URL's organic ranking position.
changefreq forces Google to use the exact specified crawl schedule.

The maintenance page mentions update information, but the specific sitemap guide says Google ignores changefreq and priority. Accurate lastmod can be used for significant updates. I would rely on that more precise current guidance.
Use 301 for temporary moves and 302 for permanent moves.
In this guide, 301 is for a permanent move and 302 is for a temporary one. I match the response to whether users and search engines should treat the new location as lasting.
Choose between them solely according to the target keyword's search volume.
Both responses always permanently replace the source URL.
Soft 404 means a temporary server overload returned as 503.
An error-like or missing-content page that does not return the appropriate missing-page status is a typical example. A useful custom error design should still return an actual 404 for a removed page.
Soft 404 is a redirect that permanently transfers content to its correct replacement.
A page that returns a genuine 404 is always a soft 404.

Implement the necessary permanent redirects and sitemap updates, then follow Google's site-move process to notify it and support recrawling and forwarding signals. Operationally, I also validate mappings and monitor results; those are implementation steps, not a promise of zero volatility.
Block the old site before Google can process its migration signals.
Redirect every old page to the new homepage and guarantee unchanged rankings.
Move the site without URL mappings, redirects or sitemap changes.
Rely only on scrolling because Google always behaves like a user.
Provide a crawlable paginated version and links to its parts. Do not rely solely on scroll-triggered requests that a crawler may not perform.
Hide all additional content behind clicks without crawlable page links.
Give every paginated section the same inaccessible fragment URL.
A multipage article is crawled only if all its pages share one URL.
rel=next and rel=prev are mandatory indexing signals.
The article's explicit requirement is prominent crawlable next and previous links. I would not invent an extra indexing requirement from that wording.
Next and previous links must be inaccessible to crawlers.
Every small site must prioritize crawl budget above all content work.
A sitemap guarantees rapid crawling regardless of site scale or server health.

When site scale, rapid change, or crawl evidence shows important content is not being processed promptly. The current linked guide gives rough scale examples and recommends simpler routine checks for sites already crawled quickly.
Crawl budget matters only when a site buys Google Ads.
Translate every version into the same URL and omit hreflang.
Treat fully translated pages as duplicates that must always canonicalize to English.
Use the appropriate multilingual/multiregional setup and hreflang annotations. Also inspect locale-adaptive responses because crawler location can determine the content Google receives.
Block all localized pages so Google chooses their language automatically.
Place state-changing actions in the sitemap to increase crawl demand.
Encourage crawling of account creation and posting actions as normal content.
Block only product detail pages while leaving cart actions crawlable.

State-changing URLs such as adding to carts or creating accounts. The maintenance guide recommends appropriate robots.txt blocks for such URLs, rather than exposing them as ordinary discoverable content.
Structured data forces display even when the page cannot be indexed.
Passing a syntax check exempts the page from quality policies.
Valid markup guarantees that the rich result will be displayed.
No. It supports understanding and eligibility for appropriate features. It must comply with general and feature-specific rules, and display is not guaranteed.
The guide covers only HTML articles and excludes images and video.
It replaces all content-specific requirements with one universal sitemap rule.
It covers only paid advertising and campaign landing pages.
Video, images, children's content, adult content, and news. News includes sitemaps, abuse prevention, paywalls, flexible sampling, snippet controls, and optional formats such as AMP or Web Stories.
PageSpeed Insights is site-wide only, while CWV is individual-page only.
Both tools exist exclusively to request Google recrawling.
The guide points to Core Web Vitals for site-wide performance information and PageSpeed Insights for inspecting individual pages. It does not say one perfect score guarantees rankings.
A perfect score in either tool guarantees first-place rankings.
Only the title tag can influence search presentation.

Implement relevant supported search features, an appropriate favicon and article dates, good titles and snippets, and applicable structured data. Use preview controls when there is a business reason to limit text or images.
Add every possible schema type regardless of the page content.
Guarantee rich features by writing a long meta keywords tag.
Unsupported browser features cannot affect Google's rendered content.
Your browser view always matches Google even with logged-in state.
A page's original HTML guarantees that every dynamic resource was processed.

The browser may use unsupported features, prior state, authentication, or resources Google cannot access. I would inspect the rendered Google view and resource access with URL Inspection or Rich Results Test.
Replace descriptive link text with empty links and no image alt text.
Give every meaningful screen one identical fragment-only navigation target.
Use click handlers without crawlable anchors or resolvable destinations.
A crawlable anchor with a resolvable destination and descriptive text, or relevant alt text for an image link. Important pages should be reachable from another findable page.
One HTML shell means individual screens need no URLs.
Put all meaningful routes behind fragments that Google cannot distinguish.
A framework's popularity guarantees discovery without internal links.

Individual content or screens need their own URLs, with discoverable links and reliably accessible rendered content. One HTML shell does not remove the requirement to address each meaningful search destination.
Resource access and browser API limitations never affect Search.
Rendering tests are useful only for sites without JavaScript.
Execution has limitations and does not prove that scripts, resources, or browser APIs expose all essential content. Testing reveals the actual output Google receives.
JavaScript execution guarantees that all content is visible and indexed.
Maintain and submit sitemaps and use available recrawl requests. If processing fails, inspect server logs and access errors. These assist discovery and reprocessing rather than guarantee rankings.
Update only the sitemap date even when page content did not change.
Repeated requests guarantee immediate ranking improvements.
Hide changed pages until Google finds them through private login sessions.
Images without text always provide all needed product context.
Remove descriptive text because it interferes with image understanding.
It provides little reliable textual explanation of what each item represents. Add relevant textual descriptions and metadata so Google and users can understand the products and page purpose.
Google requires category descriptions to exist only in image pixels.
Important text should be removed from HTML and generated only decoratively.
The guide says that CSS-generated content is not in the DOM and is ignored by Google Search. Use DOM-accessible text for substantive information; reserve CSS-generated text for decoration.
CSS content is Google's preferred place for essential product information.
CSS-generated text is always indexed as normal DOM content.
Canvas automatically supplies semantic text and metadata to Search.
Canvas-rendered copy is indexed exactly like accessible HTML text.
The guide says canvas-rendered content is not indexed as ordinary page content. Provide accessible semantic HTML text representing the important information.
Drawing text guarantees understanding without any HTML equivalent.
Google automatically knows every language and duplicate relationship.

Consolidate duplicate URLs and provide the appropriate localized-version annotations. If AMP alternatives are used, make them discoverable. Do not assume Google automatically understands every version relationship.
Force every version to redirect to one language regardless of the user.
Use noindex to identify all language alternatives.
A disallow rule can stop Google from fetching the page and seeing its noindex directive. Use a coherent method: allow crawling for noindex, or require authentication for private content.
A sitemap overrides both crawl blocking and noindex automatically.
noindex is processed before Google fetches the blocked page.
Disallow guarantees Google reads and applies the page's noindex.
Buy priority submission because missing pages cannot be diagnosed technically.
Assume backlinks are the cause before checking access or noindex.
Inspect Googlebot access with URL Inspection, review robots.txt for accidental blocking, and look for noindex in HTML. Then investigate the relevant crawling, rendering, indexing, or relevance issue.
Look only at the browser's visual design and ignore HTTP access.
Structured data guarantees a rich result for every submitted page.
Markup can describe nonexistent content if the JSON is valid.
Structured data replaces crawlability, indexing and feature-specific policies.
It can clarify meaning and make a page eligible for supported rich results. It does not guarantee display, and the markup must accurately describe the content and meet the feature's policies.
Claim every possible specialty without discussing actual experience.

Match the role to truthful experience: technical and structural audits, content strategy and development, keyword research, developer collaboration, measurement, training, and relevant market expertise. Google's list now also includes generative AI optimization.

publisher-logo-src, poster-portrait-src, title and publisher. Validate the preview rather than assuming the editor supplies all fields correctly.

Checking the visual design alone proves Google can discover and index the URL.

Responsive visual testing completely replaces AMP and Search eligibility checks.

Story media duration and audio clarity are irrelevant to creation quality.

Design only for a narrow portrait screen and ignore landscape or desktop users.

Adapt calls to action to actions readers can actually perform in the Web Story. The guide says to remove platform-specific calls to action when recreating social stories; do not leave navigation instructions that cannot work.

Google obtains all required copyright permissions for every creator.
Copyright responsibility transfers to Search when the story is indexed.
